WE MUST ADDRESS THE CLIMATE CRISIS The last 11 years have been the hottest 11 years on record. The last three years have been the hottest three years on record. 2026 will be one of the warmest years on record, and most scientists believe 2027 will be the warmest year in recorded history. This past year, Europe has seen four major heat waves, including the continent’s worst heat wave ever that killed more than 10,000 people. In the United States, three extreme heat waves exposed hundreds of millions of people to dangerous levels of heat. Drought is causing some of the lowest water levels ever seen for reservoirs along the Colorado River, threatening the drinking water of 40 million people. Puerto Ricans are being forced to ration water because of extreme drought. In Europe, some of the continent’s dryest conditions have caused major rivers to run so low that ships are running aground, nuclear power plants are shutting down, and historical artifacts that were previously submerged are being revealed. South Korea is in the midst of a record heat wave — with temperatures reaching 108.5° Fahrenheit, the highest temperature in the country’s history. China, India, Pakistan and Afghanistan are all experiencing torrential rain and flooding. As a result of rising heat levels, we are seeing massive wildfires across the world, including Oregon’s worst wildfire season and fires in Washington state that have forced nearly 65,000 families to evacuate. Europe, France and Spain are experiencing destructive wildfire seasons that have forced more than 330,000 people to evacuate their homes. Portugal, Greece, Italy, Albania, Turkey, Canada, Morocco and Algeria are also experiencing destructive wildfire seasons. This summer alone,Alaska, Louisiana, New York, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania and West Virginia have all seen record rainfall events. We’ve seen 1,000-year floods in Texas, Missouri and New York. Once rare, dangerous flash flooding emergencies are now a regular part of summer for tens of millions of Americans. One might think that, in the midst of all of this, there would be major discussions in Congress as to how best to go forward in addressing this existential crisis. Not the case. Insanely, the president of the United States continues to believe that climate change is a “hoax,” and Republican members of Congress are following their “Great Leader” over the cliff. Sadly, too many Democrats think that speaking out on climate change is “bad politics” and have remained far too silent. That has got to change. The simple truth is that we must forcefully take on the greed of the fossil fuel industry and the stupidity of Trump. The simple truth is that we can create millions of good-paying union jobs transforming our energy systems away from fossil fuels and into energy efficiency and sustainable energy. For the sake of our kids, future generations and the habitability of the planet,that is exactly what we must do.

C001035.text: Thank you, @ChuckGrassley. As Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, I worked with colleagues on both sides of the aisle to craft this stopgap funding measure. After three unnecessary lapses in funding during the fiscal year 2026 cycle, putting the possibility of yet another harmful shutdown off the table should be a priority for each and every one of us.

Tonight on the Senate floor, I urged my colleagues to support the bipartisan continuing resolution I worked with members of both parties to craft as Chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. After three unnecessary lapses in funding during the fiscal year 2026 cycle, putting the possibility of yet another harmful government shutdown off the table should be a priority for each and every one of us. This straightforward measure would keep the government funded through December 11, protect vital programs and services, and give Congress additional time to continue our work on bipartisan appropriations bills. We cannot allow another damaging shutdown to disrupt the lives of federal workers and the Americans who depend on their work.

Despite tight personal budgets, it is truly remarkable how often teachers in Maine and across the country use money out of their own pockets to purchase classroom supplies for their students. We are fortunate to have so many dedicated educators who make sacrifices to help ensure that every child has a learning environment that is safe, welcoming, and enriching. That is why I am proud to announce that the Senate today passed the Supporting Early-Childhood Educators’ Deductions (SEED) Act, a bipartisan bill I introduced with Senator Michael Bennet. The SEED Act would provide tax relief for millions of teachers by expanding the above-the-line $300 educator expense deduction, established for K-12 teachers in 2002, to include pre-K and early childhood educators. As the author of the original educator expense tax deduction for K-12 teachers, I am delighted to help lead this effort to expand this benefit to early childhood educators. We can never thank our teachers enough for all they do to prepare the next generation for success, but the Senate’s passage of this commonsense bill brings us one step closer to providing early childhood educators with well-deserved tax relief.

Today, the Senate unanimously passed my bipartisan bill with Senator Tina Smith to reauthorize the Kay Hagan Tick Act, which we first authored in 2019. Maine reported 4,257 cases of Lyme disease last year – more than three times the number of cases reported just six years ago – and 2026 is projected to set yet another record. This is a record that we do not want to set. Our bill will expand efforts to combat Lyme and other tick-borne diseases while supporting promising work already underway in Maine, including a clinical trial for a human Lyme disease vaccine at the MaineHealth Institute for Research and the University of Maine Tick Lab, where Mainers can submit ticks to be identified and tested for pathogens.

I have carefully reviewed Todd Blanche’s qualifications to be Attorney General. This includes his record and responses to questions from Senators at the Department of Justice Appropriations hearing, his confirmation hearing, and in the weeks that followed. While I believe Mr. Blanche is a capable lawyer, the Department of Justice has become increasingly political. Mr. Blanche has taken several actions that have further eroded the Department’s independence, and that is the basis for my vote to oppose his confirmation: Mr. Blanche approved an order to shield the President, his sons, and the family business from IRS audits, protections unavailable to other American taxpayers. He approved the creation of a $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund. He promised an anti-abortion organization that he would seek to prohibit the mailing of abortion medication to women nationwide. Under his leadership, the Department attempted to indict Senators Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin over their ill-advised, but constitutionally protected, videos encouraging resistance to unlawful orders. More than 1,200 former Department of Justice employees have opposed his nomination, arguing that he has undermined the institution. For these reasons, I will vote against this nomination.

B000490.text: This week, the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, appeared before the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government. During the hearing, I asked the Director about how Congress can be any clearer to ensure that the Trump Administration understands that once a funding bill is signed into law, the President is not allowed to change or second-guess the spending and withhold it due to policy or political differences. That is at the heart of Article 1 of the U.S. Constitution and why Congress also passed the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, when President Nixon tried to withhold funds that were already obligated according to the law.

This week, I asked the White House Office of Budget and Management’s Director, Russell Vought, to explain how poorly planned cuts to the federal workforce last year have weakened services and protections upon which Americans rely. This includes the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, which is responsible for protecting America’s agriculture from invasive species and diseases. USDA-APHIS began mounting a vigorous response to the resurgence of New World Screwworm – a deadly parasite affecting livestock – in 2024. However, in early 2025, the Administration illegally fired workers and forced others to resign, causing over 25 percent of all USDA-APHIS employees to leave. USDA’s New World Screwworm prevention, monitoring, surveillance, and control efforts were halted. USDA had approved $378 million in prevention and control funding for sterile fly facilities in 2023 and 2024, yet the money went unspent when the new administration paused funding. This is extremely concerning to our ranchers, and this outbreak could drive the price of food even higher. Unfortunately, we continue to see the fallout of the blunt and ill-considered cuts to federal workers, from the return of New World Screwworm to the United States, to farmers showing up to closed or understaffed Farm Service Agency offices, to attacks on our nuclear safety programs putting national security at risk. I will continue to hold the White House accountable, as I did this week during the U.S. House Appropriations Subcommittee on Financial Services and General Government hearing with Mr. Vought.

It is with heartfelt sadness that I learned of the passing of my dear friend, and magnificent former colleague, Kay Granger of Fort Worth, Texas. Some simply hold the gavel – Kay demonstrated what it meant to wield it. Her life and career were defined by a remarkable legacy of firsts: the first woman to become Mayor of Fort Worth, the first Republican woman elected to Congress from Texas, the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Defense Subcommittee, and the first woman to lead House Republicans on the Appropriations Committee. Yet, Kay never rested in the remarkableness of each milestone – she was always ready for the next responsibility, the next challenge, and the next opportunity to serve. I admired Kay Granger the moment I met her. She carried herself with an unmistakable grace, but behind her regal appearance was a razor-sharp tenacity that commanded any room. Kay demanded respect, and she got it from everyone she ever interacted with. Whip-smart and Texas tough, she had a presence that could settle any debate with little more than a look. I was lucky enough to know her personally and professionally through our work serving together in Republican leadership. So, I can attest with firsthand knowledge that ‘Don’t mess with Texas’ was more than a motto when it came to Kay. I know it well because I lost to her when we both sought the chairmanship of the Appropriations Committee previously. After that, our friendship and mutual respect didn’t change for one another. In fact, she named me to be her Vice Chair. Her mentorship and guidance were large parts of my own committee journey and helped prepare me for the privilege of succeeding her as Chairman. On the Appropriations Committee, Kay was known as a fiscal conservative, a defense hawk, and a hard – but fair – negotiator. Ever proud of her Texas roots, Granger ferociously fought for the interests of the Lone Star State. Her colleagues on both sides of the aisle always respected her professionalism, her good humor, her unfailing civility, and her willingness to strike a deal. Indeed, she and the first woman to Chair the Appropriations Committee, Nita Lowey of New York, were fast friends. They were partners who set the gold standard of how to achieve bipartisan consensus. Their portraits above our dais today remind us of the example they set and the responsibility we inherit. I will miss my friend Kay Granger. She set an unmatched standard of excellence, civility, professionalism, and dedication to duty that few can match – and no one will ever exceed. My thoughts and prayers are with Kay’s family, friends, and many admirers. We have lost a great lioness of the House, and I have lost a dear friend to whom I shall always be indebted.

C001063.text: I announced that I secured $950,000 in Community Project Funding for the City of Laredo Animal Shelter expansion. This funding marks an important step forward in the federal funding process and will help expand the shelter’s capacity to care for animals across Laredo. These federal dollars will help expand the shelter, create additional clinical and service space, improve infrastructure, and purchase equipment for examinations, vaccinations, and spay and neuter services. This investment will help provide more animals with preventive care, reduce overcrowding, support public health and safety, and give more dogs and cats a second chance at finding a loving home. I’m grateful to the Laredo Animal Care Services team, rescue partners, foster families, volunteers, veterinarians, and city leaders who work every day to care for animals in our community. I’ll continue working to bring federal resources back to TX-28 and support the people who are making Laredo a safer, stronger, and more compassionate community.

For 250 years, our great experiment has faltered, flourished, evolved, and progressed. The American experience is ever-changing and as diverse as the people who call this country home. But one thing has remained constant – the idea of America has always been a beacon of hope. Protecting this country and the ideals and values it was founded on takes work. Democracy is demanding. It takes dedication and principle. And it takes the resounding belief that upholding those ideals and values is worth the fight because America is bigger than any one person. Because liberty can only truly endure when it is paired with responsibility, virtue, and a commitment to put public good ahead of personal ambition. Today, we celebrate the moment when our founding fathers openly declared that creating this country, based in liberty, was a necessity in the face of tyranny. Their legacy is that leadership requires courage when it’s difficult, integrity when no one is watching, and a willingness to put country above self. We must remember that our duty is not merely to the next election, but to the next generation. That should be the challenge for all Americans as we look forward to another 250 years. From Massachusetts, where the fight for freedom first began, I wish you a happy 4th of July. God Bless America always, God Bless all who call her home, and God Bless our courageous men and women in uniform who continue the fight for liberty today.

On Monday, our office suffered an unimaginable loss. Chris Matthews, my District Outreach and Communications Director, passed away unexpectedly. If any one of you begin to lose faith in our country, remember Chris Matthews. Remember he was without question one of the Commonwealth’s sharpest political minds – a generational talent. Remember that he was more than a Congressional aide. He took the belief that through our actions we all can bring needed change and brought it with him on many interstate bus rides to canvas distant pivotal states and to the doors of the families he inspired. Remember through his example that public service is a genuinely noble vocation. As a trusted member of our office, he helped countless veterans, families, and those who could not advocate for themselves. Those of us privileged to have worked with him for over fifteen years will remember his laugh and his wry, often biting, humor – contrasting the way things are to the way they could be. We will always remember his authentic belief that in this country, people can bring about progress and meaningful change. It was real to him and his sincerity shown through. Chris was a genuinely good person. He was family to all of us, and we are devastated by his loss, particularly at such a young age. Our thoughts and prayers are with Molly and Eli and the many who loved him. Though we wish we had more time with him, his memory will continue to give us faith that one person can significantly make better the lives of those around him.

RT by @CongMikeSimpson: Great day at Idaho National Laboratory, one of America’s most important centers for advancing the nuclear technologies that will power our future on Earth and in space. The progress underway on SR-1 Freedom was especially exciting to see. For more than 60 years, taxpayers have invested billions in space nuclear technology. Yet America has flown just one reactor in space, and it never left Earth orbit. We’re changing that. SR-1 Freedom is our Nautilus. Like the first ship of the Nuclear Navy, it does not need to begin as the perfect end-state system. It needs to fly, establish operating experience, and give us the foundation for increasingly capable reactors and spacecraft that follow. That progress on nuclear energy can ultimately provide dependable power for the Moon Base, enable more ambitious exploration throughout the outer solar system, and help produce the spacecraft that someday carry astronauts to Mars and bring them home safely. NASA should be working on the near-impossible capabilities others are not positioned to pursue. Nuclear power and propulsion in space belongs squarely in that category. Thank you to @GovernorLittle, @CongMikeSimpson, DOE Deputy Secretary James Danly, the entire @INL workforce, and our partners at @ENERGY for the work underway to finally get America moving on nuclear power in space. SR-1 is just the beginning. The Nuclear NASA is coming.

I was glad to join farmers, producers, researchers, and ag leaders at the 65th Annual Fisher Delta Research, Extension & Education Center Field Day in the Bootheel. Farmers across southeast Missouri having been facing a tough ag economy. Commodity prices aren’t where they need to be, input costs remain too high, and producers are being squeezed from both sides. Our farmers don’t want a handout — they want the opportunity to make a living doing what they do best: feeding and fueling our country. That’s why I fought to make historic investments in American agriculture through the One Big Beautiful Bill, including stronger farm safety-net programs, increased reference prices, permanent tax relief for family farms, and provisions that give producers greater certainty to invest in their operations and plan for the next generation. But our work isn’t finished. We need to keep fighting for higher commodity prices, lower input costs, stronger and more sustainable markets, and a level playing field for American agriculture around the world. The research and innovation happening at Fisher Delta is an important part of that effort. Missouri farmers are some of the most productive in the world, and I’ll continue fighting to make sure Washington is working for them — not against them.
This is the ideology that controls today’s Democrat Party.

Pinned: This past week, I travelled throughout God’s Country and heard from the farmers and producers who feed America. One thing I consistently heard was that Southeast Missouri is better off thanks to the leadership of President Trump.

Had a great time visiting Faithful Farming in Howell County this week with Jake and Brittney Long to see the operation behind their online platform and hear how they’re building something to hand down to their sons. Jake’s family has been raising livestock on this farm since right after the Great Depression. His dad ran it as a dairy for 35 years before Jake came home from college and the family shifted to commercial beef cattle, now running about 175 cows. Between his day job as Superintendent of Howell Valley Schools and serving as a pastor, Jake’s up by 4:30 most mornings — and he and Brittney started Faithful Farming to document that life for their boys, Henry and Jack. We also discussed the threats that New World Screwworm and Theileria pose to cattle producers across our district, and I’ll continue fighting to ensure the USDA has the resources it needs to combat both. Thanks to the Working Families Tax Cuts, farms like this one can count on permanent 100% immediate expensing and a permanent small business deduction, giving them the tools to invest, grow their herd, and stay profitable year after year — so this operation can one day be handed down to Henry and Jack. I’ll keep fighting to make sure Missouri farm families have what they need to keep this way of life going.

On a six-acre farm just outside New Hope, Jessica Zander has built something our community should be deeply proud of. Helping Friendly Farm in Solebury Township is a place where children, families, and individuals with disabilities can grow, connect, and feel fully welcomed. For more than 20 years, Jessica has devoted her life to individuals with special needs, helping them build confidence, skills, and foster positive opportunities and connection. Her path began with my longtime partners at AmeriCorps, where she served as a special education teacher. From there, she continued serving in specialized mental health and special education programs, and brought therapeutic yoga and meditation to children with special needs. As a mother of children with complex medical needs, Jessica understands what so many families carry every day—the appointments, questions, advocacy, trials and tribulations, and constant search for places where their loved ones will be met with patience, respect, and understanding. So, Jessica created that place. At Helping Friendly Farm, visitors of all ages and backgrounds can pet donkeys, sit with goats, explore a sensory barn, plant seeds, play on swings, spend time in nature, and connect with animals raised to be gentle and familiar with wheelchairs and adaptive devices. It is not clinical. It is not overwhelming. It is warm, intentional, evidence-based, and full of joy, compassion, and a place where all people are seen not for what limits them, but for all they are capable of becoming. Her work reflects the kind of mission I will always fight for: ensuring that children, families, caregivers, and individuals with disabilities are seen, supported, included, and given every opportunity to thrive. Please join me in thanking and applauding Jessica and the entire HFF team for creating such an extraordinary place in our community—a true Hometown hero!

I first met Doylestown’s own Allison Hamilton in Washington last October, when she joined us with The Nature Conservancy to discuss the conservation challenges facing our region. Since then, we have continued working together on several of the conservation priorities most important to our region. Chief among them is protecting the Delaware River. As Co-Chair of the Congressional Delaware River Watershed Caucus, I am leading the bipartisan effort to reauthorize and strengthen the Delaware River Basin Restoration Program—ensuring continued investments in cleaner water, restored habitats, and the local communities and economies that depend on a healthy river system. We are also working together to advance my bipartisan Safeguarding Endangered Species Act, which would overturn the Administration’s rollback of longstanding protections against habitat destruction that kills or injures threatened and endangered wildlife. The health of our environment is inseparable from the health, character, and prosperity of our communities. Allison’s local perspective, The Nature Conservancy’s expertise, and their continued partnership are indispensable to moving this work forward. Thank you to Allison and the entire TNC team for all you do for our community, our environment, and the natural resources entrusted to our care.

Join me in congratulating two outstanding young leaders from BSA Troop 71—Sam Killenbeck of Warrington and Andrew Sueta of Doylestown—on earning the rank of Eagle Scout! Andrew drew upon his love of American history to complete his project at the Bucks County Civil War Museum, constructing courtyard benches bookended by flower planters and creating a more welcoming setting for the outdoor presentations held there. What always stands out at a Court of Honor is that no Eagle Scout reaches this milestone alone. Speaking with Sam, Andrew, their fellow Scouts, troop leaders, friends, and families, you see the full strength of the Scouting community—young people choosing to work together and serve, and an entire village of support helping them turn that commitment into something lasting. Congratulations, Sam and Andrew—and thank you to the entire PA-1 Scouting family for continuing to lead through service!

The data says otherwise: BofA shows household deposits rising across income groups this year, and the FDIC reports domestic deposits grew for a seventh straight quarter. Community banks actually outperformed the industry, posting 5% deposit growth. If the worry is the Clarity Act compromise itself, that’s backwards. Section 404 bars stablecoin issuers from paying anything that functions like interest, even disguised as rewards or points, and bans marketing stablecoins as deposits or FDIC-insured. It’s actually tougher than current law, not looser. The real story behind closing community banks isn’t stablecoins. It’s consolidation: 2,000 community banks lost in a decade, only 62 new ones formed, and the buyers are super regional banks, not crypto companies. The Banking Committee already built a nine-provision community bank package into the housing bill to help with deposit retention, on top of tightening stablecoin yield rules under Clarity. Killing the Clarity Act won’t help community banks. It just protects the status quo they say is broken.

On this day in history in 1782, George Washington created the Purple Heart during his time as the commander in chief of the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War. He awarded it to only three soldiers during the Revolutionary War. The purple badge allowed soldiers to pass guards without challenge and have their names recorded in the “Book of Merit.” The award was forgotten until it was reinstated on Washington’s 200th birthday in 1932. Today, the Purple Heart is awarded to soldiers who have been wounded, killed, or prisoners of war. It is the oldest American award for the armed forces.

On this day in history in 1945, the United States dropped the first atomic bomb on the city of Hiroshima in Japan. The U.S. began developing nuclear weapons in 1940 after learning Germany was doing the same. Although Germany was defeated before the bomb was ready, the war with Japan continued. To avoid heavy U.S. casualties, President Truman ordered the atomic bombing of Hiroshima, killing 80,000 instantly and 60,000 more from fallout. Days later, a second bomb hit Nagasaki. Japan surrendered a week later, ending World War II.

Friday in the First April Baker, a Nashville resident and founder and executive director of A Touch of the Father's Love, has spent the past 14 years ensuring that families across eastern North Carolina never have to wonder where their next meal will come from. Over the past year, A Touch of the Father's Love served more than 51,000 households and over 148,000 individuals through its unique "your choice" food pantry, which allows families to select the foods that best meet their needs. The organization also delivers food to homebound individuals and rural communities, provides pet food to families facing hardship, and partners with other nonprofits by supplying food and essential resources to help them better serve their own communities. We are proud to recognize April Baker for her unwavering dedication to serving others and strengthening communities across eastern North Carolina. Her leadership and compassion have brought hope to thousands of families, helping ensure they have access to the nutritious food and essential resources they need to live healthier, more secure lives. #FridaySpotlight

For nearly three decades, Billy Moon answered the call to serve his community, spending 28 years with the Islip Fire Department and 21 years with the FDNY. When Billy tragically lost his life in 2022, his final act was one of extraordinary selflessness: donating his organs and helping save five lives, including two retired FDNY firefighters. Billy’s story is also personal to me. His sister and I went to middle school together, and Billy was a classmate of my brother’s growing up. Yesterday, I stopped by the Hauppauge Fire Department for the New York Blood Center’s Second Annual Billy Moon Day Blood Drive, where I had the honor of catching up with Billy’s courageous wife, Kristina, and his family. Through events like this, they are ensuring Billy’s legacy of service, bravery, and selflessness continues to save and inspire others. Thank you to every donor, volunteer, and First Responder who came together today to honor Billy’s memory and carry his spirit of service forward. ❤️🇺🇸

Yesterday, after 58 years, Vietnam Veteran and U.S. Army Specialist Daniel J. Knote finally received the Purple Heart he earned after being wounded while coming to the aid of a fellow soldier in Vietnam. Daniel said, “I don’t consider myself the hero. I did my job.” That humility says everything about this American hero. He never sought recognition. He simply served his country and stood by his fellow soldier. Men and women like Daniel represent the very best of Long Island and America. Their courage and sacrifice remind us that freedom is never free. It was an honor to present Daniel with his long-overdue Purple Heart. May we never forget his sacrifice, always honor our veterans, and strive to live with the same courage and devotion to country. God bless Daniel, our veterans, and the United States of America! 🇺🇸

As a parent, I cannot imagine the grief of losing a child. No mother or father enduring that unimaginable loss should also have to worry about losing their job. Under current federal law, parents can receive job protected leave while caring for a child undergoing cancer treatment, but those protections can abruptly end if their child passes away. Long Islanders Matthew and Marissa Weippert know that heartbreak firsthand. They lost their daughter, Sarah Grace, to cancer at just 12 years old. Through the Sarah Grace Foundation for Children with Cancer, they have spent years advocating for families facing the same devastating loss. I am proud to stand with the Weipperts and parents across the country by cosponsoring H.R. 8207, which would provide up to 12 weeks of job protected leave following the loss of a child. Parents experiencing the worst moment of their lives deserve the time to grieve and be with their families without fearing for their livelihoods.

Happy 100th Birthday to World War II veteran Joseph W. Pettit of Yorktown Heights! Joe grew up in the Bronx and, at just 17 years old, left high school during his senior year to enlist in the U.S. Navy and serve our country during World War II. He served in the Pacific on Saipan and Tinian before returning home in 1946. Joe went on to finish high school, graduate from Iona College through the G.I. Bill, enjoy a successful 45-year career, and raise a wonderful family. It was an honor to celebrate this incredible milestone with Joe and recognize a life defined by family, hard work, and service to our country. Thank you for your service, and God bless our Greatest Generation. 🇺🇸

RT by @RepMaloyUtah: On Pioneer Day, I had the opportunity to tour Beaver and see firsthand the devastating impact of both wildfire and flooding. Standing in those burned and flooded landscapes, talking with the Forest Service personnel, local leaders, and the people of Beaver one thing was crystal clear: forest management works. The difference between treated and untreated forest was visible. Areas that had been thinned or otherwise managed gave firefighters a chance. They slowed the fire, reduced its intensity, helped crews establish containment lines, and in some cases, stopped the fire altogether. In the overgrown, untreated areas, the fire burned hotter, moved faster, and left behind far greater destruction, burning an unprecedented 70,000 acres in two days. It's frustrating that while the United States is the world's largest importer of lumber and paper products, millions of acres of our own forests sit overcrowded and vulnerable to catastrophic wildfire. The boots-on-the-ground Forest Service personnel managing these forests know what needs to be done and want to actively manage these lands, but too often commonsense projects are delayed or stopped by endless litigation and opposition by environmentalists and bureaucrats in Washington D.C. That's why the Fix Our Forests Act deserves to move forward. The legislation passed the House with strong bipartisan support, but has been stalled in the Senate for 18 months. It needs to move forward. I'm grateful to Congresswoman Celeste Maloy for bringing us together to see this firsthand, and to the Trump Administration officials who came to Utah to witness these conditions on the ground. With the U.S. Forest Service headquarters coming to Utah, we have a tremendous opportunity to ensure the people making decisions about our forests are closer to the landscapes and communities they serve. Thank you to USDA's Michael Boren, Sam Crofts from the Bureau of Land Management, and Chairman Bruce Westerman of the House Natural Resources Committee for taking the time to be there and hear directly from those who have been impacted by this catastrophe. On Pioneer Day weekend, that lesson feels especially meaningful. The pioneers who settled this state understood that stewardship requires hard work, planning, and taking responsibility for the land we call home. We honor their legacy not by leaving our forests untouched until they burn and cause catastrophic damage, but by actively caring for them so they remain healthy for generations to come. The Beaver community continues to show incredible resilience. I was reminded why I'm so proud to be a Utahn. We face challenges head-on, we help our neighbors, and we don't shy away from doing the difficult work that's necessary to protect our communities and our public lands. @realDonaldTrump @RepMaloyUtah @RepWesterman @SenJohnCurtis @RepBurgessOwens @RepMikeKennedy @USDA @forestservice @Interior @BLMNational @NatResources @JStuartAdams @cralbrecht52 @BeaverCountyUT

This landmark investment by the U.S. Space Force is a tremendous win for Alaska and America’s national security! The Pacific Spaceport Complex-Alaska in Kodiak is uniquely positioned to support rapid, responsive launch capabilities. I’ve had the opportunity to personally tour our Kodiak spaceport and see firsthand the incredible potential of this facility. It's clear that Alaska offers a strategic advantage few places in the world can match, with the infrastructure and geography to support the next generation of defense and space innovation. As a member of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, I am a continuous advocate for our spaceport. Today’s announcement serves as a reinforcing confirmation of Alaska’s indispensable role in America’s space economy.

This week, I had the opportunity to meet with @NASAAdmin Jared Isaacman to discuss the future of American leadership in space and the critical role Alaska will play in that mission.   As a member of the @housescience Committee, I'm committed to ensuring Alaska has a seat at the table as Congress works to support the future of America's space program.   Our nation is entering a new era of exploration in space, and Alaska is uniquely positioned to help lead the way. We discussed the tremendous potential of the Kodiak Spaceport Complex, one of the nation's critical commercial launch sites, as well as Poker Flat Research Range outside of Fairbanks, the world's only university-owned rocket range and a cornerstone of atmospheric and space research.   As investment in aerospace continues to grow, we have an incredible opportunity to prepare Alaska's students, engineers and technicians for high-paying careers right here at home. By strengthening partnerships with NASA, our universities, our military installations, and the private sector, we can ensure Alaska remains a key player in space innovation.   I appreciate Administrator Isaacman taking the time to discuss our shared vision and look forward to working together to ensure Alaska continues to serve as a vital launch point for discovery and as a key component in our nation's space leadership strategy.

H001100.text: Some places are worth taking the long way for. Our family road trip brought us to Mount Rushmore—a place I’d seen in pictures countless times, but one that feels different when you’re standing beneath it with your family. Washington, Jefferson, Roosevelt, and Lincoln each led our country through very different moments. Seeing their faces carved into the Black Hills is a pretty remarkable reminder of the history we’ve inherited—and how much of that history still shapes the country we know today. And sometimes, it’s good to experience a little history together from the road. 🇺🇸 #CO03

Colorado ranchers warned that wolf reintroduction would come with real costs. Those costs are mounting. Wolves killed or injured 13 cattle and sheep in July alone, bringing Colorado to 30 confirmed depredations this year. Several of those attacks occurred in #CO03, including in Rio Blanco, Pitkin, Eagle, and Moffat counties. Colorado Parks and Wildlife has added range riders and expanded efforts to prevent attacks, but ranchers are still losing livestock. These are families whose livelihoods are being directly affected by a policy they were right to have serious concerns about. We need to stop introducing more wolves and focus on protecting the ranchers and rural communities already dealing with the consequences. Read more about what’s happening across Western and Southern Colorado here: https://www.coloradoan.com/story/news/local/colorado/2026/08/05/colorado-wolf-attacks-on-livestock-hit-record-pace-after-deadly-july/91146744007/?gnt-cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=false&gca-epti=z114541p119550l002850c119550u003441e005000v114541&gca-ft=18&gca-ds=sophi

Ninety years ago, farmers in the Grand Valley had a problem: the power lines didn’t reach their homes and farms. So they came together and built their own solution. It’s a story that says a lot about Western Colorado: when something needs to get done, neighbors find a way to do it. In the late 1800s, dozens of Hungarian families moved from Pennsylvania's coal mines to Haralson County to establish a wine-making community.  They named their village Budapest after the Hungarian capital, and planted vineyards across the surrounding hillsides.  After Prohibition was enacted in the 1920s, many of the families left, and all that remains from that era is a home which once served as a Catholic rectory and the historic Budapest cemetery.  Today, we visited both. Ambassador Takács' visit is a special moment in Haralson County's rich history, and I am grateful for the incredible support the Haralson County Historical Society, the Hungarian Community Church of Georgia, the Dogwood Hills team, and local officials and community leaders provided to facilitate this meaningful event. Thank you, Ambassador Takács, for visiting Georgia's 3rd Congressional District, and thank you for strengthening the relationship between Hungary and the United States of America! @HungaryinUSA

We announced the finalized Cooperative Interstate Shipment (CIS) agreement, giving qualifying Georgia state-inspected meat processors the opportunity to ship USDA-labeled products across state lines. This is a tremendous victory for Georgia's farmers, ranchers, and small meat processors. Yesterday, Georgia became one of only a handful of states participating in the Cooperative Interstate Shipment Program—allowing qualifying state-inspected meat processors to ship USDA-labeled products nationwide. For too long, a handful of massive processors have dominated the market, putting family-owned processors at a disadvantage. This is another step toward expanding opportunity, strengthening rural America, increasing competition, and rebuilding America's food production capacity. Under Biden, the United States flipped from net agricultural exporter to net importer. Four years of weakness turned a historic American strength into a strategic vulnerability. We’re fixing that. Food security is national security. Thank you Georgia!!! 🥩🐂🇺🇸

Thank you for the warm welcome, @MichealMartinTD. Together, we will strengthen Europe's competitiveness. A massive increase in EU spending is not sustainable for Germany, and we are calling for spending cuts. Europe will only succeed through its own economic strength.

Was für eine abscheuliche Tat in Berlin. Hunderttausende Menschen aus aller Welt feierten friedlich beim Christopher Street Day. Sie wollten, dass wir gut und tolerant miteinander umgehen. Das ist ein Angriff auf unsere Gesellschaft.

WORLD_FRANCE_PRESIDENT.text: Face au terrible séisme qui a frappé la Colombie, j’adresse, au nom de la France, mes pensées les plus sincères au peuple colombien. Je pense aux victimes, à leurs familles, aux blessés et à toutes celles et ceux qui ont été touchés par cette catastrophe. Notre solidarité va également aux équipes de secours et à tous ceux qui œuvrent, avec courage, pour venir en aide aux populations sinistrées. Dans cette épreuve, la Colombie peut compter sur notre amitié et notre soutien.

Félicitations à Demi Vollering, vainqueure du Tour de France Femmes ! À chaque étape, un même engouement et une ferveur populaire pour faire vivre cette grande fête du cyclisme mondial. Une course qui rassemble, une fierté française.

À Kyiv et dans sa région, la Russie a une nouvelle fois choisi de cibler des civils. Cette politique de terreur, menée à coups de missiles et de drones, est inacceptable. Chaque nouvelle attaque renforce une évidence : la Russie doit payer le prix de son agression et répondre de ses crimes. Aux côtés de l’Ukraine, nous ne céderons ni à la lassitude ni à l’intimidation. L’Union européenne et ses partenaires continueront d’accroître la pression sur la Russie, notamment par de nouvelles sanctions, tout en renforçant le soutien militaire à l’Ukraine afin qu’elle puisse se défendre et protéger sa population.
